messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rahul had always been an active person, enjoying his work as a physical therapist and spending his free time hiking with his wife. But everything changed on that fateful day two years ago when he was involved in a severe car accident on his way home from work. The sound of screeching tires and crunching metal still echoed in his mind, and the image of his crumpled car haunts him to this day. Since then, Rahul has been plagued by unwanted thoughts about the accident, often waking up in the middle of the night with a start, his heart racing, as if he's reliving the moment. These nightmares have become more frequent, leaving him feeling on edge and constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of threat. He finds himself noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects everywhere - a broken glass on the floor, a sharp rock on the hiking trail, a stranger's eyes lingering too long on him. His difficulty concentrating has also made it challenging to focus on his work, leading to mistakes and frustration. As Rahul struggles to make sense of these symptoms, he has come to believe that his body has been permanently damaged by the accident. He fears that he can no longer trust his own body, that it's unreliable and prone to injury. This fear has led him to mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios, constantly preparing himself for the next disaster. He also finds solace in compulsive cleaning and organizing, as if a tidy environment can somehow counterbalance the chaos within him. But these strategies only provide temporary relief. The more Rahul scans his surroundings for threats, the more he notices potential dangers - a loud noise makes him jump, a stranger's sudden movement sends his heart racing. This constant threat monitoring reinforces his negative appraisals: "I'm vulnerable," "my body can't be trusted." And so, the cycle continues. As Rahul navigates this treacherous landscape, he finds himself withdrawing from activities and social interactions that once brought him joy. He avoids loud noises, crowded spaces, and even hiking with his wife, fearing that another accident might happen. His relationship with his wife has become strained as a result, leaving Rahul feeling isolated and trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear and hypervigilance. Despite his best efforts to manage these symptoms on his own, Rahul has finally realized that he needs help. He's been avoiding seeking therapy for too long, fearing that it would somehow confirm his worst fears - that he is indeed broken, beyond repair. But the prospect of living with these debilitating symptoms forever has become unbearable. With a deep breath, Rahul takes the first step towards seeking help, hoping to break free from this cycle and learn to trust himself once again.
